processing: Made exactly like Tieguanyin: light oxidation and ball-rolling with a light dry for the green style, or a light to medium roast for the traditional style.
harvest_season: Spring (late April to May) and autumn (October), typically a few days ahead of Tieguanyin.
appearance_dry: Tight green pellets that look much like Tieguanyin but a little smaller and lighter, with a slender stem.
appearance_wet: Oval leaves that are thinner than Tieguanyin's, with a paler red edge and a thin stem with knobbly joints like bamboo.
taste_profile: Orchid and a lighter, slightly sharper sweetness than Tieguanyin, a thinner body and a shorter, clean finish.

brewing.notes: Rinse once, then short steeps in a porcelain gaiwan with water just off the boil. Treat it as a Tieguanyin that fades a steep or two sooner.

vintage_note: Sold like Tieguanyin by the spring and autumn harvests of the current year, in vacuum packs, and best within the year kept sealed and cold. It is usually somewhat cheaper than Tieguanyin from the same village and is often not labelled at all, because much of it is blended into or sold as Tieguanyin.
description:
Ben Shan is Tieguanyin's quiet twin: an Anxi cultivar from the same town as Tieguanyin, made the same way, looking almost the same in the bag, and a good deal of it is sold under Tieguanyin's name. Drunk under its own name it is an honest, lighter, cheaper Anxi oolong.

The cultivar comes from Yaoyang village in Xiping, the same township that gave the world Tieguanyin, and by the traditional account it was identified there around 1870. It is one of the four main Anxi cultivars alongside Tieguanyin, Mao Xie and Huang Dan, and because it grows faster and yields better than the fussy Tieguanyin bush, farmers like it. It is processed identically: light oxidation, repeated ball-rolling and a light dry for the green style, or a roast for the traditional one.

Telling the two apart takes a little practice. Ben Shan's pellets are slightly smaller and lighter, the wet leaf is thinner and more oval, and the stem is the giveaway: slender, with knobbly joints like a bamboo cane, where Tieguanyin's is stouter. In the cup Ben Shan has a similar orchid aroma but a thinner body, a sharper sweetness and a finish that ends sooner, without the creamy weight and long cool aftertaste that mark a good Tieguanyin.

Brew it like Tieguanyin, short steeps with water just off the boil, and expect five or six good infusions. It is an easy daily oolong, and in a side-by-side tasting it is the fastest way to learn what people are paying for in Tieguanyin.

It is sold by season, spring and autumn, and should be drunk within the year, kept cold. Honest sellers label it and price it below Tieguanyin; if an Anxi Tieguanyin seems cheap for its grade, Ben Shan in the blend is the likeliest reason, which is a reason to buy from people who tell you.
sources_note: The Yaoyang / Xiping origin and the circa 1870 date are from the traditional Anxi account.
history:
Ben Shan comes from Yaoyang in Xiping, Anxi county, the same area tied to Tieguanyin. Its early record is a 1937 survey of the Anxi tea trade by Zhuang Canzhang, quoted in a modern article, which says the tea was found about sixty years before, around 1870, by someone named Yuan Xing. The plant was therefore also called the Yuan Xing variety. The original survey was not seen here.

It was approved as a national improved variety at the 1984 cultivar conference and is counted among the four main se zhong, with Huang Dan, Mao Xie and Mei Zhan. It is a close relative of Tieguanyin with stronger growth and adaptability, and its likeness to that tea has led merchants to sell it under the more famous name.
